# forge v0.10.0 — what each workspace is doing, on whose account, on which ports

Everything below has landed since v0.9.1. Most of it you will see; the largest
part of it you will not, because it was the inside being rebuilt so that Forge
can run somewhere other than a laptop.

## What each workspace is doing, and what it costs

A workspace tells you what it is working on, in Claude's own words, and the topic
outlives the session that wrote it — so a tab you last touched on Tuesday still
answers the first question you have about it. Beside it: which Claude login it
runs on, how much context it has left, and how close that account is to its rate
limit, because a limit belongs to an account and not to a workspace. And two
clocks — how long the session has been going, and how much of that you actually
spent here.

## Ports that belong to a workspace

Every workspace owns a block of host ports, assigned once and never moved. That
immutability is the point: the same number means the same service forever, so it
can be written into a compose file, an OAuth redirect or a CORS whitelist and
stay correct. What a workspace publishes inside its block is tunnelled to your
machine without being asked, and the ports panel turns them into links you click.

Workspaces made before this get their block with `forge ports assign` — which the
installer now runs for you.

## The nightly clean-up actually reclaims

A host running the old timer nightly still reached 98% full, with every run
exiting 0. `--filter until=24h` on the build cache measures *last used*, not age,
and on a build server almost every record is touched daily — so it spared nearly
all of it. The cache is now pruned unfiltered, an unused-volume sweep can be
opted into, and a run that leaves the disk still full **fails** instead of
reporting success. Silence was half the problem.

## Servers you cannot reach directly

`forge host add root@10.0.0.5 --alias=box --jump=bastion`, and the same flag on
`host prepare`, because a server on a private network has to be reachable before
it can be provisioned. It is `ssh -J` and it means what `-J` means: the jump host
opens a plain stream and the SSH session happens over it end to end, so the
bastion carries your bytes and never reads them. Kept in Forge's own config
rather than left to `~/.ssh/config`, so both clients — and eventually a phone,
which has neither — follow the same route.

## The client and the server say which build they are

`forge version` answers for this machine, and `forge version <alias>` for the
agent on a server. They can differ, and that difference is worth knowing: the
agent rides inside the client and gets onto a host by being uploaded, so a host
runs whatever client last prepared it.

`forge host update [alias]` puts this build's agent where it is not. It
provisions nothing — no packages, no docker, no firewall, no keys — and the
installer calls it, so the two halves stay in step without anyone remembering to
do it.

`forge ui [start]` brings the port tunnels up with it. The ports panel offers every
published port as a link to this machine, and each of those is carried by a
tunnel the forwarding supervisor holds — a UI without it lists addresses that do
not answer. Stopping the UI leaves them running: they serve the machine, not the
window.

## Also in the UI

A host shell and a local shell in the rail beside the workspace one. Every
server's CPU, memory and disk under the file tree. A side pane that reads: plain
identity, one line per server, dots with one meaning each.

And a side pane that holds still. What the tab you have open answers — the tree
and its ports — sits above what every session shares, so switching tabs moves as
little as it can. The logins are listed by name rather than by whichever is
closest to a limit, which used to reorder them while you worked. A server's icon
stays with its own figure instead of drifting toward the next one's. And the eye
over the session clocks hides the times, not the banner they live in.

## Rebuilt inside, with nothing to see

Forge grew a core — one package holding the operations, with the CLI and the
browser as two thin front ends over the same actions rather than one calling the
other. Terminals and the file browser moved behind that boundary, the state
directory and the device key became things you hand in rather than things the
code assumes, and the UI can now start inside somebody else's process.

Alongside it, an SSH client of Forge's own, built on `golang.org/x/crypto/ssh`:
commands, terminals asked of the server instead of wrapped around an `ssh`
process, port forwards as listeners rather than subprocesses, a trust store that
records a host on first sight, and jump hosts. It is **off** — `ssh` is still what
Forge runs — and turns on with `FORGE_SSH_BACKEND=go`. It is what will let Forge
run where there is no `ssh` binary at all.

## Upgrading from v0.9.1

```sh
curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Marb-AI/forge/main/install.sh | sh
```

The installer stops the daemons it finds running (with the build that started
them), replaces the binary by rename rather than writing over it, updates the
agent on every server it knows, gives a block to workspaces that have none, and
starts back only what was up. `FORGE_SKIP_AGENT_UPDATE=1` opts out of the parts
that touch your servers.

One manual step, this time only:

```sh
forge host prepare <ssh-target> --alias=<alias>
```

The fixed nightly clean-up is installed by the provisioner, so it needs one run
to land. Repeat any flags you used the first time (`--no-firewall`,
`--no-ssh-harden`, `--no-docker-prune`): prepare does what you tell it, not what
you told it last time. It touches no container and no tmux session, and docker is
not restarted.

Nothing else changes on a server, no keys are created or rotated, and your
`~/.ssh` is still how Forge reaches it.
